h1: Starting a brewpub in Southeast Asia: what founders plan for
title: Starting a Brewpub in Southeast Asia | Craft Beer School
desc: Heat, humidity, water, imported malt and licensing: what founders plan for before opening a brewpub in Southeast Asia, from site to the first brew.
teaser: Hot, humid and import-dependent: a Southeast Asian brewpub is a cooling, water and logistics problem before it is a recipe problem.
standfirst: Southeast Asia has an enthusiastic craft audience and a hard operating climate. These are the decisions that separate a brewpub that runs from one that fights its own building.
sections: Heat is the first design constraint

A warm, humid climate loads every part of the plant. Fermenters need cooling all year, not just in summer. The cold room works harder every time the door opens. Size glycol chilling for the warmest day, not the average one. Give the compressor room to breathe. A fermenter that cannot hold 18 °C on a hot afternoon will cost you beer.

Ale yeast ferments cleanly at moderate temperatures, so brewpubs in hot places often lean on ales and on strains chosen for warm fermentation. Lagers are possible, but only with proper chilling.

Ventilation matters as much as chilling. A brewhouse releases steam during the boil. In a humid building that steam condenses on walls, ceilings and electrics. Extraction above the kettle and a dehumidified cold room keep mould and corrosion down.

A fermentation that runs too hot makes solvent-like fusel alcohols and heavy fruity esters, so choose strains with warm fermentation in mind.
Water quality varies city to city

Municipal water in the region ranges from soft and clean to heavily chlorinated. Ask for a water report. Plan a carbon filter to remove chlorine and chloramine before the water reaches the mash. Chlorine and its by-products can give a medicinal, plastic flavour in finished beer.

See water use per litre of beer for how to track use once you are running.

Ask whether the supply varies by season. Some cities change treatment during heavy rain. A water report from last year may not describe this month. Test pH and hardness yourself with a simple kit before each season. Adjust mash pH to the 5.2 to 5.6 range with acid or salts once you know what the water is doing.
Malt, hops and the supply line

Most specialty malt and hops arrive by sea freight. Containers take weeks. Malt picks up moisture in a humid store. Keep sacks off the floor, sealed and out of the sun. Mill only what you need for the brew. Hops want a cold, dark, oxygen-free store.

Local cereals such as rice can lighten body and suit the climate. They need cooking before mashing, so confirm your brewhouse can do it.

When a container arrives, check the malt for moisture and insects before it goes into the store. A small test mill and a sample of crushed grain tell you quickly whether it has softened. Hops should arrive cold. A delivery that sat on a warm dock should be queried with the supplier before you accept it.
Licensing and the rules around alcohol

Rules differ widely across the region. Some countries or states restrict alcohol heavily. The usual chain applies where alcohol is legal: company registration, premises approval, production and sales licences, then duty registration. Where it is restricted or banned, local law comes first. A non-alcoholic product may be the only route.

Do not rely on a blog for the current rules. Ask the national regulator or a licensing adviser. Ask in writing.

Ask what the licence lets you do on site. In some places a brewpub may sell only what it brews. Food rules may also apply separately. Our guide on licensing steps most countries share lays out the shape of the process.

Serving temperature matters more in a hot room. Beer poured at 3 to 6 °C stays crisp for a few minutes on a warm terrace. Beer poured warmer turns flat and sweet fast. Check that serving tanks, lines and taps hold temperature. Insulate any long run between the cold room and the bar.

Keg lines that pass through a hot ceiling void foam badly. A short, cold line with a cold bar beats a long line with a strong pump.

Food drives a brewpub as much as beer. Beer that works with local cooking, spice and sweetness tends to sell. That usually means cold, clean and refreshing. Heavy, high-strength beers sell more slowly in hot weather, so use them as a small part of the range.

Track what sells by the week with a simple demand forecast so you brew to the real pattern and not to hope.

Tourist trade can matter in cities with visitors, but it comes and goes. Build a base of regulars first, then treat visitors as extra.
Data you will want from week one

A log of brew dates, fermentation temperatures, tank volumes and packaged volumes shows you where beer and money go. Start with the few fields you will actually use and add more only when a question needs them.
faqs: Can I brew lagers in Southeast Asia?
Yes, if your chilling can hold lager fermentation temperatures of roughly 8 to 13 °C all year. Many brewpubs start with ales and add lagers once cooling capacity is proven.
For many styles it is, because specialty malts are mostly made elsewhere. Plan for long lead times and humid storage. Use local cereals where they suit the style.
Is alcohol legal everywhere in the region?
No. Rules vary by country and sometimes by state. Check with the national regulator or a licensing adviser before you plan a brewpub.
